blocks.text:
Transfer to the airport for your flight to Puerto Natales, then continue by road to Torres del Paine National Park.

After a few days in the cities, the route heads to Patagonia in Chile’s far south. You have two full days ahead among granite towers, lakes, rivers and glaciers.

After breakfast, take a tour of Torres del Paine National Park.

The granite towers of Paine rise more than 2,000 metres above the Patagonian steppe. Before the park was established in 1959, this land was used extensively for sheep grazing. Its ecosystems took a long time to recover from intensive farming.

Beyond the towers, the park has blue lakes, forest trails, fast-flowing rivers, footbridges, glaciers and waterfalls. It has been part of UNESCO’s network of biosphere reserves since 1978. Wildlife includes rheas, Andean condors, flamingos and guanacos.

The tour also includes the Mylodon Cave, about 25 kilometres from Puerto Natales. Remains of ancient animals were discovered here in 1895, including a sabre-toothed cat, an American horse and the giant ground sloth Mylodon darwini, which lived in the area 8,000–10,000 years ago. A sculpture of the sloth stands at the entrance.

Open steppe meets steep granite massifs in Torres del Paine. The lakes range in colour from grey-blue to bright turquoise, and the weather can shift quickly from sunshine to strong winds and cloud. Guanacos often graze in the open, and you may spot condors high above them. The drive, short walks and stops by the water each show you a different part of the park over the course of the day.

The park covers more than 242,000 hectares. Along the way, you’ll see lakes, ice-covered mountains and waterfalls. A walk of about 15 minutes takes you to Salto Grande, the waterfall connecting Lakes Nordenskjöld and Pehoé.

The return drive passes the Río Serrano and Lakes Toro and Porteño. Overnight at the hotel.
